steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) are both nucleic acids built from nucleotide sub-units, but they differ in chemistry, structure, stability, and biological role. Below is a concise, side-by-side comparison followed by brief explanations.

1. Sugar component  
   • DNA: 2-deoxyribose (lacks an –OH on the 2′ carbon).  
   • RNA: Ribose (has an –OH on the 2′ carbon).

2. Nitrogenous bases  
   • DNA: Adenine (A), Guanine (G), Cytosine (C), Thymine (T).  
   • RNA: A, G, C, Uracil (U) in place of thymine.

3. Strandedness and overall shape  
   • DNA: Usually double-stranded with antiparallel strands forming a long, uniform double helix (B-form in cells).  
   • RNA: Usually single-stranded; folds back on itself to form diverse secondary/tertiary structures (hairpins, loops, cloverleaf, etc.). Some viruses have double-stranded RNA genomes.

4. Chemical stability  
   • DNA: More chemically stable; the absence of the 2′-OH and double-helix protection make it less prone to hydrolysis and UV damage is easier to repair.  
   • RNA: Less stable; the 2′-OH can attack the backbone (intramolecular hydrolysis), making RNA more transient.

5. Typical cellular localization  
   • DNA: Confined mainly to nucleus (eukaryotes), mitochondria, and chloroplasts.  
   • RNA: Synthesized in nucleus but functions largely in cytoplasm (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA); also found in nucleolus and many organelles.

6. Primary biological role  
   • DNA: Long-term, heritable storage of genetic information; template for its own replication and for RNA synthesis.  
   • RNA: Several operational roles—messenger (mRNA), adaptor (tRNA), catalytic/structural (rRNA), regulation (miRNA, siRNA, lncRNA), genome of some viruses, and ribozymes.

7. Replication vs. transcription/translation  
   • DNA is replicated (DNA → DNA) once per cell cycle with high fidelity.  
   • DNA is transcribed into RNA (DNA → RNA). RNA is then translated into protein (RNA → protein) or functions directly (ribozymes, regulatory RNAs).

8. Lifespan  
   • DNA: Can persist for the life of the cell or organism; chromosomes last generations.  
   • RNA: Often short-lived (minutes to hours for mRNA), though some RNAs (e.g., rRNA, tRNA) are more stable but still routinely turned over.

9. Repair mechanisms  
   • DNA: Cells devote extensive machinery (excision repair, recombination, mismatch repair) to fix damage.  
   • RNA: Generally not repaired; damaged RNA is degraded and replaced by new transcripts.

10. Modifications  
   • DNA: Cytosine methylation (5-mC) is most common; influences gene regulation.  
   • RNA: Dozens of base/sugar modifications (m6A, pseudouridine, 2′-O-methylation) fine-tune stability, localization, and translation.

11. Ability to act as an enzyme  
   • DNA: Mostly inert structurally; not known to catalyze reactions.  
   • RNA: Some RNAs (ribozymes, the ribosome’s peptidyl-transferase center) can catalyze biochemical reactions.

12. Historical/biochemical perspective  
   • DNA’s stability suits it for storing instructions across generations (the “hard drive”).  
   • RNA’s versatility (information carrier, scaffold, catalyst) supports the “RNA world” hypothesis—that early life relied on RNA before DNA and proteins evolved.

Summary sentence: At the molecular level, the critical distinction is the 2′-OH group on ribose and the uracil base of RNA, which confer chemical lability and structural flexibility, allowing RNA to function dynamically in information transfer and catalysis, while DNA’s deoxyribose, thymine, and double-helix architecture provide a robust, long-term repository for genetic information.
